# eSIM and connectivity

## eSIM China: Best Plans Compared (Airalo, Holafly & Nomad)

Source: https://chinalayoverguide.com/guides/best-esim-for-china/
Last updated: 2026-09-10

> Reviewed 2026-09-10. eSIM plans, prices, and fair-use policies change often: check each provider's current terms before buying. Providers listed as examples, not endorsements.

## The quick recommendation

**For a short China layover, buy a 3–5 GB travel eSIM before you fly: most people will be happiest with Airalo for price and reliability, or Holafly if you want unlimited data and built-in VPN routing without thinking about it.**

The single most important fact first: **China's network blocks Google, WhatsApp, Instagram, Facebook, and sometimes Gmail.** A travel eSIM is the fix that requires no VPN app and no technical know-how: because your data is routed through a partner network *outside* mainland China, the blocked apps just keep working.

## Why the stakes are higher for layovers

A layover traveler has exactly one shot to get this right. Airport Wi-Fi in China usually demands an SMS code your home number may not receive, so if your eSIM isn't installed before you land, you're navigating a strange city with no maps, no translation, and no way to reach anyone. Buy it at home, install it on home Wi-Fi, test it before you take off. That one habit matters more than *which* provider you pick.

## The three providers, compared

| | **Airalo** | **Holafly** | **Nomad** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Best for** | Price + dual-network reliability | Unlimited data + built-in VPN routing | Fixed-data at the lowest starting price |
| **Plans** | 1–20 GB, 7–30 days | Unlimited, 1–90 days | 1–10+ GB, typically 30 days |
| **Typical pricing** | ~$5 (1 GB) to ~$40 (20 GB) | ~$19–99 by days | ~$4–35 |
| **Network** | China Unicom + China Mobile (dual) | China Mobile (single) | Varies by plan |
| **Firewall bypass** | Yes (routes outside mainland China | Yes) marketed as "VPN included" | Yes, routes outside mainland China |
| **Hotspot** | Generally allowed | Limited (500 MB/day) | Varies |
| **Support** | App chat (can be slow) | 24/7 live chat, fast | In-app |

**Prices are indicative and change.** Always compare the *exact plan* you're buying, not the brand name.

## Which one should you pick?

**Buy Airalo if:** you want the best balance of price and reliability, and you're comfortable managing a data allowance. The dual-network coverage (China Unicom + China Mobile) is genuinely more reliable when you're moving between cities. 3–5 GB is the right size for a layover and will cover maps, messaging, and light media.

**Buy Holafly if:** you don't want to think about data caps or VPN setup, and you're willing to pay a premium for peace of mind. Unlimited data plus built-in VPN routing is the simplest possible setup, zero decisions after install. You pay roughly 1.5–2x the cost of equivalent fixed data, but for a short trip the absolute difference is small.

**Buy Nomad if:** you're budget-sensitive and your usage is light and predictable. Nomad's fixed-data plans often start at the lowest price per trip. The trade-off is single-network coverage and fewer hand-holding features.

## How much data do you actually need?

For a layover of up to 48 hours, with maps, translation, photos, and video calls:

- **1 GB/day** is a comfortable rule of thumb.
- A **3 GB plan** covers a full-day layover with room to spare.
- A **5 GB plan** covers a multi-day stopover or heavy WhatsApp-video use.

Heavy streaming in China on unlimited plans can still hit fair-use throttling (Holafly throttles after ~90 GB/month. You'd have to be streaming constantly to hit it).

## Five things to check before you buy

1. **Your phone is unlocked and eSIM-capable.** This kills more plans than anything else.
2. **The plan routes outside mainland China.** This is *the* feature that keeps Google and WhatsApp working. All three providers above do this, but not every eSIM on the market does.
3. **Activation timing.** "Starts on install" vs "starts on first connection" differs by provider. Know which one you're buying.
4. **Refund policy.** Holafly is generous (6 months, but connection problems must be raised *during* the trip); Nomad is 30 days if never activated. Understand yours before you pay.
5. **Hotspot limits.** Holafly caps hotspot at 500 MB/day. If you plan to tether a laptop, check first.

## The step-by-step (works for any provider)

1. **Buy the eSIM at home** and install it on reliable Wi-Fi. You'll get a QR code.
2. **Name the plan** in your phone settings (e.g. "China travel").
3. **Turn off your home SIM** or disable data roaming on it to avoid surprise charges.
4. **Enable the travel eSIM** right before landing, many plans activate on first connection.
5. **Test before you leave the airport:** open Google Maps and WhatsApp in the terminal.

## Bottom line

For a China layover, the provider decision is secondary to the habit: **buy it early, install it early, test it before you take off.** If you want to stop thinking about it, buy Airalo's 3–5 GB plan for the best balance, or Holafly for unlimited data with zero setup friction. Both keep your everyday apps working the moment you land: which is the whole point.

For the full setup walkthrough, see [China eSIM setup: do it before you land](/guides/esim-setup-before-you-land/).

**Frequently asked questions**

### Which eSIM is best for a China layover?

Any plan that routes data outside the mainland firewall, because that is what keeps Google Maps, WhatsApp and Gmail working. Compare on routing and hotspot support rather than headline price, and install it before you fly.

### How much data do I need for a short layover?

For a layover of a day or two, a modest plan is usually enough. Maps, translation and messaging use little data; video and large uploads are what burn through it. Check whether the plan throttles after a daily cap, since that matters more than the total.

### Do I need a VPN as well as an eSIM?

Usually not. A travel eSIM that routes data outside mainland China already gets you to the apps you need. A VPN is a separate tool for when you are on local Wi-Fi or a local SIM instead.

### Can I install a China eSIM after I land?

Technically yes, but it is a bad plan. You need working internet to download the profile, and airport Wi-Fi in China typically requires an SMS code you may not be able to receive. Install and activate it before departure.

**Sources**

- Airalo — China eSIM plans (example provider, not an endorsement): https://www.airalo.com/china-esim
- Holafly — China eSIM (example provider, not an endorsement): https://esim.holafly.com/esim-china/
- Nomad — China eSIM (example provider, not an endorsement): https://www.getnomad.app/china-esim

## China Airport Wi-Fi: The SMS Catch (and How to Stay Online)

Source: https://chinalayoverguide.com/guides/china-airport-wifi/
Last updated: 2026-09-16

## The short answer

Chinese airports do offer free Wi-Fi, but it is usually **gated behind an SMS code sent to a Chinese mobile number**. If you are on a foreign SIM, that code often never arrives. **Do not plan on getting online at the airport**: buy a travel eSIM before you fly and activate it on landing.

## Why the Wi-Fi gate exists

Chinese public networks require real-name registration. In practice that means:

1. Connect to the airport SSID.
2. Enter a phone number to receive a verification code.
3. Enter the code to get online.

Step 2 is where foreign travelers get stuck. Some airports accept international numbers; many do not reliably. Roaming SMS can also be delayed or blocked entirely.

Some airports provide a **kiosk that scans your passport** to issue a login code instead. Availability varies by terminal, and there may be a queue.

## What actually works

| Option | Works on arrival? | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Travel eSIM activated before landing** | ✅ Yes | The reliable answer |
| Airport Wi-Fi with foreign number | ⚠️ Sometimes | Do not depend on it |
| Passport-scan kiosk | ⚠️ Sometimes | Queue, terminal-dependent |
| Local SIM bought at the airport | ✅ After purchase | Needs a counter visit and passport registration |
| Roaming on your home SIM | ✅ Yes | Expensive but works |

## The five-minute fix

Before you fly:

1. **Buy a travel eSIM** and install it on home Wi-Fi, see [Best eSIM for China](/guides/best-esim-for-china/).
2. **Test it** is not possible until you land, so instead confirm the install completed and the plan shows as active.
3. **Enable it** just before landing.
4. **Open a map** in the terminal to confirm data is flowing.

This removes the entire problem: you never need the airport Wi-Fi code.

## If you arrive without data

1. Look for the airport's **Wi-Fi kiosk** or a staffed information desk.
2. Ask airport staff, many terminals have a help desk that can issue a code.
3. Use a **coffee shop or lounge** network; some are less strictly gated.
4. As a last resort, **buy a local SIM** at a carrier counter (bring your passport).

## Bottom line

Airport Wi-Fi in China is a trap for foreign travelers, available, but gated behind a code you may not be able to receive. Buy and install an eSIM before you fly so you land with data. See the [eSIM setup guide](/guides/esim-setup-before-you-land/) and the [apps checklist](/guides/china-apps-checklist/).

**Frequently asked questions**

### Does airport Wi-Fi in China require a phone number?

Yes, in most Chinese airports. The network typically asks for a Chinese mobile number to send an SMS verification code, which many foreign travelers cannot receive.

### Can I use airport Wi-Fi with a foreign phone number?

Sometimes, but it is unreliable. Some airports accept international numbers and some do not, and roaming SMS often fails. Do not plan your arrival around being able to get online at the airport.

### What should I do instead of relying on airport Wi-Fi?

Buy a travel eSIM before you fly and activate it on landing. That gives you working data the moment you clear immigration, without needing a Wi-Fi code or a Chinese phone number.

### Is there free Wi-Fi at Chinese airports at all?

Yes, most major airports offer free Wi-Fi, but it is gated behind SMS verification or a passport scan at a kiosk. The gate is the problem, not the availability.

**Sources**

- Beijing Capital International Airport — official site: https://www.bcia.com.cn/
- Shanghai Airport — official transport information: https://www.shanghaiairport.com/

## China Apps Checklist: What to Install Before You Fly

Source: https://chinalayoverguide.com/guides/china-apps-checklist/
Last updated: 2026-09-16

## The short answer

Install **five categories of app before you fly**: payments (Alipay + WeChat), navigation (Amap), ride-hailing (DiDi), translation, and trains if you are moving between cities. Do it on home Wi-Fi: Google Play is blocked in China and app-store behavior changes once you connect to a Chinese network.

## The checklist

### 1. Payments, do this first

| App | Why | Priority |
|---|---|---|
| **Alipay** | Works almost everywhere; the best foreign-card support | Essential |
| **WeChat** | Backup payment rail, plus tickets and bookings run through mini-programs | Essential |

Verify your passport and link a card in both. See [Alipay for foreigners](/guides/alipay-for-foreigners/) and [WeChat Pay](/guides/wechat-pay-and-tenpaygo-for-foreigners/).

### 2. Navigation, Google Maps will not save you

| App | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Amap (高德地图)** | Best English support of the Chinese maps; reliable transit directions |
| **Baidu Maps** | Excellent Chinese-language coverage |

Google Maps is blocked and its China data is often inaccurate. Download an offline map area as a backup. See [does Google Maps work in China?](/guides/does-google-maps-work-in-china/)

### 3. Ride-hailing

| App | Notes |
|---|---|
| **DiDi** | China's Uber. English interface, foreign phone numbers, international cards |

DiDi also runs as a mini-program inside Alipay and WeChat if you would rather not install another app. See [DiDi and ride-hailing for foreigners](/guides/didi-and-ride-hailing-in-china/).

### 4. Translation

| App | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Google Translate** | Download the offline Chinese pack before you fly; online mode may be blocked |
| **Baidu Translate** | Works inside China without a VPN; strong camera mode |

Camera translation is the feature you will actually use, menus, signs, taxi addresses.

### 5. Trains and travel (if you are moving between cities)

| App | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Trip.com** | Easiest for foreigners; books with a passport, English interface |
| **12306** | The official railway app; cheaper, but clunkier for foreign cards |

See [China high-speed rail for tourists](/guides/china-high-speed-rail-for-tourists/).

## Set it up in this order

1. **At home, on Wi-Fi:** install everything, create accounts, verify your passport in Alipay and WeChat, link your card.
2. **At home:** download offline maps and the offline Chinese translation pack.
3. **Before boarding:** confirm each app opens and is logged in.
4. **On landing:** enable your eSIM and test a map search.

## The one that catches people out

**SMS verification.** Many apps want to text you a code. If your home SIM is off or roaming SMS is unreliable, you cannot complete setup abroad. Do every verification step **before you leave**, and write down the last four digits of your registered phone number: DiDi drivers ask for them as an identity check.

## Bottom line

Ten minutes of setup at home removes almost all the friction of a China layover. Payments, maps, ride-hailing, translation, trains, install them all before you fly, and read [China eSIM setup](/guides/esim-setup-before-you-land/) to make sure they work when you land.

**Frequently asked questions**

### What apps do I need for a trip to China?

The essentials are a payment app (Alipay, plus WeChat Pay as backup), a map app that works in China (Amap or Baidu Maps), a ride-hailing app (DiDi), a translation app with camera mode, and a train app if you plan to travel between cities.

### Can I install these apps after I land in China?

Technically yes, but do not plan on it. Google Play is blocked in mainland China, the Apple App Store may serve a different storefront, and SMS verification is unreliable while roaming. Install everything on home Wi-Fi before you fly.

### Does Google Maps work in China?

Google Maps is unreliable in mainland China because Google services are blocked. Navigation data is also often inaccurate or offset. Use Amap or Baidu Maps instead: both work well, though Amap has the better English support.

### Do I need a VPN app for China?

If you use a travel eSIM that routes data outside mainland China, you usually do not need a separate VPN for everyday apps. If you use a local Chinese SIM, you will need one for Google, WhatsApp, and Instagram, and VPN apps are hard to install once you are in China.

**Sources**

- Alipay — official site: https://www.alipay.com/
- Amap (Gaode) — official site: https://www.amap.com/
- China Railway 12306 — official ticketing: https://www.12306.cn/en/index.html

## Does Google Maps Work in China? (And What to Use Instead)

Source: https://chinalayoverguide.com/guides/does-google-maps-work-in-china/
Last updated: 2026-09-29

## The short answer

**No, Google Maps is not reliable in mainland China.** Google services are blocked, and China's mapping data is often offset or incomplete anyway. Use **Amap (高德地图)** or **Baidu Maps** for navigation, and keep Google Maps only as something that might work over a travel eSIM.

## What's blocked and what isn't

| Service | On a local Chinese network | Over a travel eSIM |
|---|---|---|
| Google Maps | Blocked | Usually works |
| Gmail | Blocked | Usually works |
| WhatsApp | Restricted | Usually works |
| Instagram / Facebook / X | Blocked | Usually works |
| Amap / Baidu Maps | Works | Works |
| Alipay / WeChat Pay | Works | Works |
| Apple Maps | Partially works | Partially works |

Apple Maps is a partial exception. It is available on iPhones in China and uses local data, though detail and English quality vary.

## Why "it loads" does not mean "it works"

China's mapping coordinates are deliberately offset from global GPS standards. That means even when Google Maps renders, **the pin can sit in the wrong place** relative to the real street. This is a well-known cause of travelers being dropped at the wrong entrance or the wrong side of a river.

Use a Chinese map app and the problem disappears.

## The map apps that actually work

| App | Language | Best for | Availability |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Amap** (Gaode, 高德地图) | English available | The default for foreign visitors: metro, bus and walking directions, and finding a place by its English name | Works everywhere in mainland China |
| **Baidu Maps** (百度地图) | Chinese-first | Finding a Chinese address, deepest local coverage | Works everywhere in mainland China |
| **Apple Maps** | Localised | iPhone users who want the built-in app | Partly works in China on local data; detail and English quality vary |
| **Google Maps** | English | Nothing useful while you are on a Chinese network | Only over a travel eSIM, and the coordinate offset still applies |

**Install Amap before you fly.** The reason is not convenience, it is that app-store behaviour inside China is unpredictable, and you do not want to be solving it on airport Wi-Fi. Both Amap and Baidu Maps are free.

**Amap (Gaode)**
- Best English support among the Chinese map apps.
- Reliable metro, bus, and walking directions.
- Good for finding a destination by its English name.

**Baidu Maps**
- Deepest coverage of Chinese addresses.
- Strong once you can paste or scan a Chinese address.

Both handle the coordinate-offset problem natively, which is the part Google Maps cannot fix.

## Will a travel eSIM bring Google back?

**Usually, yes.** A travel eSIM from Airalo, Holafly, or Nomad routes your data through a partner network **outside** mainland China, so Google Maps, Gmail, and WhatsApp frequently keep working with no separate VPN. That is the main reason travelers buy an eSIM rather than a local SIM, see [Best eSIM for China](/guides/best-esim-for-china/) and [eSIM vs VPN vs roaming](/guides/esim-vs-vpn-vs-roaming/).

Two caveats:

1. **Coverage varies.** Some providers and some plans route differently.
2. **Even working Google Maps has the offset problem.** Use Amap for anything where the exact entrance matters.

## Practical navigation setup

1. Install **Amap** and **Baidu Maps** at home, before you fly, see the [China apps checklist](/guides/china-apps-checklist/).
2. Download an **offline map area** for each city you will visit.
3. Save your hotel's **Chinese address** as a screenshot. It works for taxis and DiDi.
4. Keep a **translation app with camera mode** for signs and menus.

## Bottom line

Treat Google Maps as unreliable in China and Amap as your default. If you want Google services back for messaging and email, a travel eSIM is the simplest route. Read the [eSIM setup guide](/guides/esim-setup-before-you-land/) before you fly.

**Frequently asked questions**

### Is Google Maps blocked in China?

Google services are blocked in mainland China, so Google Maps generally does not load or update reliably. Even where it partially works, its China mapping data can be inaccurate or offset.

### What should I use instead of Google Maps in China?

Use Amap (Gaode) or Baidu Maps. Amap has the better English interface and solid public-transit directions; Baidu Maps has deep Chinese-language coverage. Download an offline area before you fly as a backup.

### Does a travel eSIM make Google Maps work in China?

Often yes. Travel eSIMs from providers like Airalo, Holafly, and Nomad route your data through a network outside mainland China, so Google services frequently keep working without a separate VPN.

### What is the best map app for China?

Amap (Gaode). It has the best English support of the Chinese map apps, reliable metro, bus and walking directions, and will find a destination by its English name. Baidu Maps is the fallback when you have a Chinese address to paste. Apple Maps partly works on iPhones in China. Do not rely on Google Maps while you are on a Chinese network.

### Is WhatsApp blocked in China?

WhatsApp is restricted in mainland China on local networks. It typically works over a travel eSIM that routes internationally, or over a VPN. Instagram, Facebook, and X are similarly restricted.

**Sources**

- Amap (Gaode) — official site: https://www.amap.com/
- Airalo — China eSIM plans (example provider, not an endorsement): https://www.airalo.com/china-esim

## China eSIM Setup: Do It Before You Land

Source: https://chinalayoverguide.com/guides/esim-setup-before-you-land/
Last updated: 2026-09-16

> Reviewed 2026-09-16. eSIM plans and prices change often: check the provider's current terms before buying.

## Why you need this before you land

China's network blocks many apps you use every day, Google services, WhatsApp, Instagram, Facebook, and sometimes Gmail. There are two ways around it:

1. **A travel eSIM** (recommended): your data is routed through a partner network outside China, so blocked apps keep working without a VPN.
2. **A local Chinese SIM**: fast and cheap, but blocked apps stay blocked unless you also set up a VPN.

The catch: **airport Wi-Fi in China usually requires an SMS code**, and your home number may not receive it. Set everything up before departure, not in the arrivals hall.

## Before you buy

- Confirm your phone is **unlocked** and supports **eSIM**.
- Check how much data you'll want: maps, translation, and video calls burn data. 1 GB/day is a comfortable starting point for a layover traveler.
- Check coverage for the cities you'll visit (most plans cover all of mainland China).

## Setup steps, in order

1. **Buy the eSIM at home** and install it while you still have reliable Wi-Fi. Most providers give you a QR code.
2. **Name the plan** in your phone settings (e.g. "China travel") so it's easy to find later.
3. **Turn off your home SIM** or disable data roaming on it to avoid surprise charges.
4. **Enable the travel eSIM** right before landing, or switch it on after you land. Many plans activate on first connection.
5. **Test before you leave the airport**: open Google Maps and WhatsApp while still in the terminal.

## On the ground

- Keep your home SIM off. If your phone asks about "allow data switching", say no.
- Most travel eSIMs are **data-only**. You won't get a Chinese phone number. That's fine: you don't need one for Alipay/WeChat Pay, maps, or ride-hailing.
- If an app asks for SMS verification and you can't receive it, use your home number's roaming SMS if available, or set up the app before you travel.

## Bottom line

A travel eSIM is the highest-leverage thing you can do before a China layover: it keeps your usual apps working and removes the biggest source of airport stress. Buy it early, install it early, and test it before you take off.

- [China airport Wi-Fi: the SMS catch](/guides/china-airport-wifi/)
- [China apps checklist: what to install before you fly](/guides/china-apps-checklist/)
- [Payments in China for foreigners](/guides/payments-in-china-for-foreigners/)

**Frequently asked questions**

### Why do I need an eSIM before landing in China?

Because the apps you rely on are blocked on local networks, and you need working data the moment you land for maps, translation and ride-hailing. An eSIM that routes data outside the mainland keeps those apps working.

### When should I install and activate my eSIM?

Install the profile before you fly, at home, on reliable Wi-Fi. Activate it so it is ready on arrival, or set it to activate on landing if your provider supports that.

### Will my regular SIM still work?

Your home SIM keeps working for calls and texts if you leave it enabled, but its data will not bypass the firewall. Use the eSIM for data and keep the physical SIM for receiving verification codes.

### Can I get a Chinese eSIM instead?

Chinese carriers sell local SIMs and eSIMs, but those route through mainland networks, so the apps you need stay blocked without a VPN. For a short layover, a travel eSIM is the simpler choice.

**Sources**

- Airalo — China eSIM plans (example provider, not an endorsement): https://www.airalo.com/china-esim
- Holafly — China eSIM (example provider, not an endorsement): https://esim.holafly.com/esim-china/
- Nomad — China eSIM (example provider, not an endorsement): https://www.getnomad.app/china-esim

## VPN for China: eSIM vs VPN vs Roaming Compared

Source: https://chinalayoverguide.com/guides/esim-vs-vpn-vs-roaming/
Last updated: 2026-09-16

## The short answer

**For a layover, a travel eSIM wins.** It is cheaper than roaming, needs no VPN, and keeps your usual apps working. Roaming is the easiest if money is no object. A VPN is only essential if you plan to use a local Chinese SIM.

## Side by side

| | Travel eSIM | VPN | Home-carrier roaming |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Setup** | Install before you fly | Install and test before you fly | Nothing to do |
| **Keeps Google/WhatsApp working** | Usually yes (routes outside China) | Yes, if it works | Often yes |
| **Cost** | Low (a few dollars per GB | Subscription on top of data | Highest) often per-day fees |
| **Reliability in China** | High | Variable; can be throttled or blocked | High |
| **Needs a VPN too?** | No | It *is* the VPN | No |
| **Best for** | Most travelers | Local-SIM users, longer stays | Very short trips, one-app users |

## How each one works

### Travel eSIM
Your data is routed through a partner network **outside mainland China**, so the Great Firewall is not in the path. That is why Google Maps, Gmail, and WhatsApp usually just work. Plans are typically 1–20 GB; 3–5 GB is plenty for a layover. See [Best eSIM for China](/guides/best-esim-for-china/).

### VPN
A VPN tunnels your traffic out of China. It works, but it can be unstable: providers get throttled, and some are blocked entirely. **The critical rule: install and test it before you fly.** VPN provider websites and app stores are hard to reach from inside China.

### Roaming
Your home carrier's roaming agreement often routes through a foreign network, so blocked apps may keep working with zero setup. The problem is price: daily roaming passes commonly cost more per day than a travel eSIM costs for the whole trip.

## The combinations that make sense

- **Short layover, want it simple:** travel eSIM only.
- **Local SIM for a cheap Chinese number:** local SIM **+** a pre-installed VPN.
- **Multi-country trip:** a regional eSIM covering China plus your next countries.
- **Emergency backup:** keep roaming enabled on your home SIM but data-off, so you can receive SMS codes.

## The rule that matters most

**Whatever you choose, set it up at home.** Airport Wi-Fi in China usually requires an SMS code your home number may not receive, and app stores behave differently once you are on a Chinese network. Install before you fly, see [China eSIM setup](/guides/esim-setup-before-you-land/) and the [apps checklist](/guides/china-apps-checklist/).

## Bottom line

Buy a travel eSIM for the trip, skip the VPN unless you are using a local SIM, and treat roaming as a backup for SMS codes rather than your data plan. For providers, see [Best eSIM for China](/guides/best-esim-for-china/).

**Frequently asked questions**

### Do I need a VPN if I have a travel eSIM in China?

Usually not. Travel eSIMs route your data outside mainland China, so Google, WhatsApp, and Instagram typically keep working without a separate VPN. If you use a local Chinese SIM, you will need a VPN.

### Does roaming work in China?

Yes, and it is the simplest option, your home carrier's roaming often routes through a foreign network, so blocked apps may keep working. The catch is cost: daily roaming passes are usually far more expensive than a travel eSIM.

### Should I buy a VPN before going to China?

If you plan to use a local SIM, yes, install and test it before you fly, because VPN providers are hard to reach once you are inside China. If you use a travel eSIM, a VPN is usually unnecessary.

### What is the cheapest way to stay connected in China?

A travel eSIM is typically the cheapest and simplest option for a short trip. A 3–5 GB plan costs a fraction of a week of daily roaming, and it bypasses the firewall without extra setup.

**Sources**

- Airalo — China eSIM plans (example provider, not an endorsement): https://www.airalo.com/china-esim
- Holafly — China eSIM (example provider, not an endorsement): https://esim.holafly.com/esim-china/

# Airport transfers and logistics

## China Airport to City: Transfers Compared for Every Major Layover Hub

Source: https://chinalayoverguide.com/guides/china-airport-to-city-transfers/
Last updated: 2026-09-16

## The short answer

Every major Chinese airport connects to its city by **metro or a dedicated express train**, usually for under ¥35. **The metro is almost always the right default**; taxis and DiDi are for late arrivals, heavy bags, or groups. Budget **60–90 minutes** door to door and be back **2.5 hours** before an international departure.

## The numbers, airport by airport

| Airport | Best option | Time | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Shanghai Pudong (PVG) | Maglev + Metro Line 2 | ~40–55 min | ¥50 + ¥4 (¥40 with boarding pass) |
| Shanghai Pudong (PVG) | Metro Line 2 direct | 60–90 min | ¥7–9 |
| Shanghai Hongqiao (SHA) | Metro Lines 2 / 10 | 30–50 min | ¥3–7 |
| Beijing Capital (PEK) | Airport Express | 25–35 min | ¥25 |
| Beijing Daxing (PKX) | Daxing Airport Express | 30–40 min | ¥35 |
| Guangzhou Baiyun (CAN) | Metro Line 3 | ~45–55 min | ~¥8 |
| Chengdu Tianfu (TFU) | Metro Line 18 | 35–40 min | ¥7–10 |
| Xi'an Xianyang (XIY) | Airport bus Line 1 | ~40–50 min | ~¥25 |
| Chongqing Jiangbei (CKG) | Metro Line 10 | 40–50 min | ~¥6 |
| Shenzhen Bao'an (SZX) | Metro Line 11 | ~30–50 min | ~¥7–10 |
| Hangzhou Xiaoshan (HGH) | Metro / Airport bus | ~45–60 min | ~¥20–30 |

Treat fares and journey times as indicative. They change, so check the airport's own transport page or a maps app on arrival.

## How to choose

- **Daytime, light luggage:** metro or express train. Cheapest and traffic-proof.
- **Heavy bags or a group:** taxi or DiDi, especially from Pudong.
- **Late arrival:** taxi or DiDi only; the metro has stopped.
- **A cross-airport connection** (for example Shanghai PVG to SHA, or Beijing PEK to PKX): allow **1.5–2 hours** and do not also plan sightseeing.

## Paying for the ride

- **Metro and Maglev:** buy a single ticket with cash, or use Alipay/WeChat Pay QR at the gates. Shanghai gates also accept contactless foreign cards.
- **Taxi:** metered; pay with cash or a QR app. Most drivers do not take foreign cards.
- **DiDi:** China's ride-hailing app. Fares are shown upfront and international cards are supported. You need a data connection, see [eSIM setup](/guides/esim-setup-before-you-land/).

## Rules that save you money and trouble

- **Use the official taxi queue**, never a driver soliciting inside arrivals.
- **Have your destination in Chinese characters** on your phone.
- **Avoid airport currency exchange**; use an ATM at a major bank instead (see [do you need cash in China?](/guides/do-you-need-cash-in-china/)).
- **Check the last train time** before you count on the metro.

## Bottom line

China's airport transfers are cheap, fast, and well signed in English. Pick the metro unless you land late or carry a lot, and always check the last service time before you rely on it. Next, see [what you can do in each layover window](/cities/).

## Related guides

- [Luggage storage at China's airports](/guides/luggage-storage-at-china-airports/)
- [DiDi and ride-hailing in China](/guides/didi-and-ride-hailing-in-china/)
- [China high-speed rail for tourists](/guides/china-high-speed-rail-for-tourists/)
- [China apps checklist: what to install before you fly](/guides/china-apps-checklist/)
- [Is China safe for tourists? Scams and risks](/guides/china-travel-safety-and-scams/)

**Frequently asked questions**

### What is the fastest way from Shanghai Pudong Airport to the city?

The Maglev to Longyang Road takes about 8 minutes, then Metro Line 2 continues into the center: roughly 40–55 minutes door to door for around ¥55. Metro Line 2 direct is cheaper (¥7–9) but takes 60–90 minutes.

### How do I get from Beijing Capital Airport to the city?

Take the Airport Express to Dongzhimen or Sanyuanqiao (about 25–35 minutes for ¥25) then metro or taxi onward. It runs roughly 06:00 to 23:00.

### What is the cheapest way from a Chinese airport to the city?

The metro. Fares from most airports are under ¥10, though the trip is slower than the dedicated express trains or Maglev. Hongqiao (SHA) is the cheapest and easiest, at ¥3–7 and 30–50 minutes.

### What if I land after midnight?

Metro and Maglev services stop between roughly 21:40 and 22:30. After that, use a metered taxi or DiDi from the official queue or app, never an unofficial driver soliciting in arrivals.

**Sources**

- Shanghai Airport — official transport information: https://www.shanghaiairport.com/
- Beijing Capital International Airport — official site: https://www.bcia.com.cn/
- Beijing Daxing International Airport — official site: https://www.bdia.com.cn/

## China High-Speed Rail for Tourists: Booking with a Passport

Source: https://chinalayoverguide.com/guides/china-high-speed-rail-for-tourists/
Last updated: 2026-09-16

## The short answer

China's high-speed rail is fast, punctual, and easy for foreigners. You book with your **passport** as the ID and board by scanning it at the gate. Book through **Trip.com** if you want English and a foreign card, or the official **12306** app if you want the source of truth. Arrive **45–60 minutes early**; stations are big and security is mandatory.

## Why it matters for a layover

High-speed rail turns a stopover into a real trip. From Shanghai you can reach **Hangzhou** (West Lake) in about an hour. From Beijing, **Xi'an** is roughly 4.5 hours (feasible inside a 240-hour transit window. Within the transit rules you must still respect the **permitted areas** and exit through a **designated port**) see the [ports and permitted areas reference](/guides/240-hour-transit-ports-and-permitted-areas/).

## How to book

| Method | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| **Trip.com** | English interface, foreign cards, easy refunds | Small booking fee |
| **12306 (official)** | Cheapest, definitive | Clunkier for foreign cards, Chinese-first UX |
| **Station counter** | Works when nothing else does | Queue, language barrier |

Both online options require **your passport details**. Book a few days ahead for popular routes and holidays: the good departures sell out.

## Seat classes

| Class | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Second class** | Perfectly comfortable; the default choice |
| **First class** | Wider seats, quieter carriage |
| **Business class** | Lie-flat, expensive, rarely worth it for a day trip |

## At the station

1. **Arrive 45–60 minutes early.** Major stations are the size of airports.
2. **Security screening** is mandatory for all bags.
3. **Scan your passport** at the gate, e-tickets mean no paper ticket is needed.
4. **Find your carriage and seat** on the platform displays.
5. **Boarding closes shortly before departure**, do not cut it fine.

## Practical tips

- **Your passport is your ticket.** Keep it accessible, not buried in a bag.
- **Note your train number** (e.g. G1234). That is what signage and staff use.
- **Store bags in the racks** at the carriage ends; overhead space is limited.
- **Food:** a trolley and sometimes a dining car, but bring your own for short hops.
- **Same-day returns** are easy on short routes like Shanghai–Hangzhou.
- **Do not plan tight rail connections before an international flight**: leave a real buffer.

## Fares to expect

Indicative second-class fares:

| Route | Time | Fare |
|---|---|---|
| Shanghai → Hangzhou | ~1 hour | from ~¥73 |
| Beijing → Xi'an | ~4.5 hours | ~¥515+ |
| Guangzhou → Shenzhen | ~35 min | ~¥75 |
| Chengdu → Chongqing | ~1.5 hours | ~¥154 |

Fares and schedules change: check 12306 or Trip.com before you plan around them.

## Bottom line

High-speed rail is one of the best things about traveling in China and it works smoothly for foreigners. Book with your passport, arrive early, and use it to extend a layover into a genuine trip. Pair it with [DiDi](/guides/didi-and-ride-hailing-in-china/) for the last mile to the station.

**Frequently asked questions**

### Can foreigners book China high-speed rail tickets online?

Yes. You can book through the official 12306 app or through Trip.com, using your passport as the ID document. Trip.com is easier for foreign cards; 12306 is the official source and is usually cheaper.

### Do I need to print a train ticket in China?

Generally no. China moved to e-tickets, you scan your passport at the station gate. Some travelers still print a receipt for expense purposes, but it is not required to board.

### How early should I arrive at a Chinese train station?

Arrive 45–60 minutes before departure. Stations are large, security screening is mandatory, and passport gates can queue. Boarding typically closes a few minutes before departure.

### Is high-speed rail in China expensive?

Second class is good value, for example, Shanghai to Hangzhou is about an hour and starts around ¥70–75, and Beijing to Xi'an is roughly 4.5 hours. First and business class cost significantly more.

**Sources**

- China Railway 12306 — official ticketing: https://www.12306.cn/en/index.html
- National Immigration Administration (NIA) — visa-free transit policies: https://en.nia.gov.cn/n147418/n147463/c183412/content.html

## Is China Safe for Tourists? Scams, Risks, and What to Actually Watch For

Source: https://chinalayoverguide.com/guides/china-travel-safety-and-scams/
Last updated: 2026-09-16

## The short answer

**China is a very safe country for tourists.** Violent crime against visitors is rare and city streets are safe at night. The risks you actually face are petty and predictable: **taxi overcharging, tourist scams near major sights, and pickpocketing in crowds.** Handle those and you will be fine.

## The real risks, ranked

### 1. Unlicensed taxis at airports
Touts approach you in arrivals offering a "taxi". They overcharge heavily.

**Avoid it:** use the **official taxi queue** or book **DiDi**. Never follow someone who approaches you. See [DiDi and ride-hailing](/guides/didi-and-ride-hailing-in-china/).

### 2. The "tea ceremony" and "art student" scams
Near major tourist sights, friendly English-speaking strangers invite you to a tea ceremony, an art exhibition, or a student practice session. The bill at the end is enormous.

**Avoid it:** decline unsolicited invitations from strangers, however friendly. Real invitations do not come from someone who approached you on the street.

### 3. Aggressive touts
Souvenir sellers, "massage" touts, and photo hustlers cluster around landmarks.

**Avoid it:** a firm "no thanks" and keep walking. Do not engage, do not follow.

### 4. Pickpocketing in crowds
Metro stations and night markets at peak hours.

**Avoid it:** front pockets or a zipped bag, and be aware when squeezed into crowds.

### 5. Overpriced "tour" offers
Door-to-door tour sellers offering Great Wall or city tours at inflated prices.

**Avoid it:** book through a reputable platform in advance, or organize it yourself.

## The genuine safety rules

- **Use DiDi or the official taxi queue.** Never an unmarked car.
- **Keep your passport secure** and carry a photocopy or photo separately.
- **Save your embassy details offline** before you travel.
- **Do not carry large amounts of cash**, see [do you need cash in China?](/guides/do-you-need-cash-in-china/).
- **Watch your step**, traffic, e-bikes, and scooters are the most likely way to actually get hurt.
- **Respect local rules** at attractions and on public transport.

## Emergency numbers

| Service | Number |
|---|---|
| Police | **110** |
| Ambulance | **120** |
| Fire | **119** |
| Traffic accident | **122** |

## Health and practicalities

- **Tap water is not drinkable**, drink bottled or boiled water.
- **Pharmacies** are common; bring any prescription medication in original packaging with a copy of the prescription.
- **Travel insurance** is cheap and worth having for a longer stopover.
- **Air quality** in northern cities can be poor in winter; sensitive travelers should plan indoor stops.

## Bottom line

China is safer than most travelers expect. Your job is not to defend against violence. It is to avoid petty hustles by sticking to official channels: the taxi queue or DiDi, licensed attractions, and pre-booked transport. For getting around safely, see [China airport-to-city transfers](/guides/china-airport-to-city-transfers/).

**Frequently asked questions**

### Is China safe for foreign tourists?

Yes. Violent crime against tourists is rare, and Chinese cities are generally safe to walk at night. The realistic risks are petty: taxi overcharging, tourist-oriented scams, and pickpocketing in crowds.

### What are the most common scams in China?

The classic ones are unlicensed taxis at airports, the 'tea ceremony' or 'art student' invitation near major sights, and aggressive souvenir or massage touts. All are avoidable by using official channels and declining unsolicited invitations.

### Is it safe to walk around at night in China?

Generally yes in major cities. Streets are well lit and busy, and violent crime is uncommon. Use normal precautions in nightlife areas, and use DiDi rather than unmarked cars.

### What should I do in an emergency in China?

Dial 110 for police, 120 for an ambulance, and 119 for fire. Keep your embassy's contact details saved offline, and keep a photocopy of your passport separate from the original.

**Sources**

- National Immigration Administration (NIA) — official English portal: https://en.nia.gov.cn/
- DiDi — official international rider information: https://www.didiglobal.com/

## DiDi and Ride-Hailing in China: A Guide for Foreigners

Source: https://chinalayoverguide.com/guides/didi-and-ride-hailing-in-china/
Last updated: 2026-09-16

## The short answer

**DiDi (滴滴出行) is China's Uber**, and it is the easiest way for a foreigner to get around. It has an English interface, accepts foreign phone numbers, and can be paid with an international card or through Alipay. Set it up **before you fly**, because SMS verification and app stores are unreliable once you are in China.

## Set it up

1. **Install the right app.** Search for **"DiDi Chuxing" (滴滴出行)**: the domestic China app. The separate international "DiDi Rider" app does **not** work in mainland China.
2. **Switch to English** in *Settings → Language*.
3. **Register with your phone number** and enter the SMS code. Do this at home on your own network.
4. **Add a payment method** under *Me → Wallet → Payment Methods*. Add a card, and enable auto-deduct.
5. **If the card fails**, link it in Alipay instead and choose Alipay as your DiDi payment method. That path is usually more reliable.

## Booking a ride

1. Check the **pickup pin**, drag it to where you are actually standing, not across the road.
2. Enter your destination. English names work for major hotels and landmarks; pasting a **Chinese address** is more reliable for smaller places.
3. Choose a ride type:

| Type | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Express (快车)** | Cheapest, fine for almost every trip |
| **Premier (专车)** | Nicer car, good for airports |
| **Taxi (出租车)** | Hails a metered taxi through the app |
| **Express Pool (拼车)** | Shared, cheaper, slower |

4. Confirm and wait: typically 2–5 minutes in city centers.
5. **Before getting in: check the plate number matches the app.** If it does not, cancel.

## The "last four digits" ritual

Drivers commonly ask for the **last four digits of your registered phone number** as an identity check. Write them down or keep them handy in a note, easier than saying numbers in a language you may not speak.

## Prices to expect

| Trip | Approximate fare |
|---|---|
| Short central trip (3–5 km) | ¥15–30 |
| Cross-city (15+ km) | ¥50–100 |
| Airport to city (Shanghai) | ¥150–250 |

Fares are shown before you confirm, and surge pricing applies at rush hour, in bad weather, and on holidays.

## If you'd rather not install another app

**DiDi runs inside Alipay and WeChat** as a mini-program. Open Alipay, tap the **Transport** area, and choose Taxi/Ride-hailing. You get the same driver pool with one less app, and Alipay's foreign-card handling is often smoother. See the [China apps checklist](/guides/china-apps-checklist/).

## Staying safe

- **Match the plate** before boarding, every time.
- **Use Share Trip** to send your route to someone.
- **Ignore touts** at airport exits offering rides, unlicensed and overpriced.
- **Use the official pickup zone** (follow signs for *Online Car-hailing / 网约车*).
- **Lost an item?** Use the in-app lost-item feature and offer a small reward.

## Bottom line

DiDi is the single most useful transport app for a China layover. Install it at home, link a card (or Alipay), check the plate, and you can move around a Chinese city without speaking a word of Mandarin. For airport runs specifically, see [China airport-to-city transfers](/guides/china-airport-to-city-transfers/).

**Frequently asked questions**

### Can foreigners use DiDi in China?

Yes. DiDi has an English interface, supports registration with an international phone number, and accepts international cards in many cases. Alipay and WeChat Pay can also be used as the payment method, which is often more reliable.

### Do I need a Chinese phone number for DiDi?

No. You can register with a foreign number and receive the SMS code, though roaming SMS is sometimes unreliable, register before you fly. DiDi also runs as a mini-program inside Alipay and WeChat.

### What if my card does not work in DiDi?

Link your card to Alipay first and set Alipay as the DiDi payment method. Alipay's foreign-card processing is generally more robust than DiDi's direct card binding.

### Is DiDi cheaper than a taxi in China?

Usually yes, and the fare is shown before you confirm. Expect roughly ¥15–30 for a short central trip and ¥150–250 for an airport run into Shanghai.

**Sources**

- DiDi — official international rider information: https://www.didiglobal.com/
- Alipay — official site: https://www.alipay.com/

## Hotel Registration for Foreigners in China: The 24-Hour Rule

Source: https://chinalayoverguide.com/guides/hotel-registration-for-foreigners-in-china/
Last updated: 2026-09-16

## The short answer

Foreign visitors to China must **register their accommodation with the local police within 24 hours of arrival**. If you stay in a hotel, the hotel does it for you at check-in. If you stay privately, **you are responsible** for registering yourself.

## How it works

| Where you stay | Who registers | When |
|---|---|---|
| Hotel | The hotel, at check-in | Within 24 hours of arrival |
| Guesthouse or hostel | The property, usually at check-in | Within 24 hours |
| A friend's or family's home | You, or your host | Within 24 hours |
| Rented apartment | You (or the host) | Within 24 hours |

Hotels that accept foreign guests handle the paperwork automatically. You simply hand over your passport. The catch is that **not every property is registered to take foreign guests**, which is why it is worth confirming before you book.

## If you are staying privately

You (or the person hosting you) must go to the **local public security bureau** office and register. Bring your passport and your host's ID. Many areas now offer an **online self-registration system** for foreign nationals, but availability varies by city, so ask locally or check the NIA.

## Why it matters for a layover

On a short stop this is easy to overlook: especially if you are staying with a friend or in a short-term rental rather than a hotel. It is a legal requirement, and skipping it can mean **fines** and complications with immigration. It also matters if you are on **visa-free transit**: officers may ask where you are staying, and an unregistered or out-of-area address can cause problems.

## Practical tips

- **Book foreigner-registered hotels** for a stress-free arrival.
- **Carry your passport**. It is needed for registration and can be requested by authorities.
- **Do it on day one.** Do not wait until the end of your stay.
- **Keep a record** of the registration slip or confirmation if you are given one.

## Bottom line

Registration is a simple 24-hour obligation that hotels handle for free. If you are not in a hotel, make it your first task after arrival. For the entry rules themselves, see [240-hour visa-free transit](/guides/240-hour-visa-free-transit/).

## Related guides

- [China airport to city: transfers compared](/guides/china-airport-to-city-transfers/)
- [Luggage storage at China's airports](/guides/luggage-storage-at-china-airports/)
- [Is China safe for tourists? Scams and risks](/guides/china-travel-safety-and-scams/)
- [240-hour visa-free transit: the complete guide](/guides/240-hour-visa-free-transit/)

**Frequently asked questions**

### Do I have to register my accommodation in China as a foreigner?

Yes. Foreign nationals must register where they are staying with the local public security office within 24 hours of arrival. If you stay at a hotel, the hotel does this for you at check-in.

### Do hotels register foreign guests automatically?

Foreigner-registered hotels complete the registration at check-in. Confirm your hotel accepts foreign guests, and keep your passport with you, it is used for registration.

### What if I stay with a friend or in an apartment?

You, or the person hosting you, must register with the local police station within 24 hours. Many areas now offer an online self-registration system, but check the local rules.

### What happens if I do not register?

Failing to register can lead to fines and problems with immigration. It is a legal requirement, not a formality, so make sure it happens within 24 hours.

**Sources**

- National Immigration Administration (NIA) — official English portal: https://en.nia.gov.cn/
- National Immigration Administration (NIA) — Policy interpretation of visa-free transit policies (2025-07-04): https://en.nia.gov.cn/n147418/n147463/c183412/content.html

## Luggage Storage at China's Airports: What It Costs and Where to Find It

Source: https://chinalayoverguide.com/guides/luggage-storage-at-china-airports/
Last updated: 2026-09-24

## The short answer

Every major Chinese airport has **left-luggage counters (行李寄存)**, typically **¥15–30 per bag per day**. Bring your passport, keep the receipt, and you are free to explore. If you are taking a private car or DiDi, the best storage is often **the boot of the car**: the driver waits and you skip the queue entirely.

## Your options, ranked

| Option | Cost | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| **Keep bags in your DiDi / private car** | Free (included in the fare) | Wall trips, multi-stop days |
| **Airport left-luggage** | ¥15–30 per bag per day | Public-transport layovers |
| **Hotel storage** | Free if you are a guest | Overnight stopovers |
| **Station lockers / counters** | Similar to airports | Rail connections |
| **Carry a small backpack only** | Free | Short layovers, fastest |

## How airport left-luggage works

1. Find the **行李寄存** counter: usually in the arrivals or departures hall; airport signage is in English.
2. Show your **passport**; they may also want your onward ticket.
3. Pay per bag per day and **keep the receipt/tag**. You need it to collect.
4. Collect with time to spare; queues form before evening departure banks.

Prices vary by airport and by bag size. Treat ¥15–30 as indicative and check the counter's own board.

## The option most travelers miss

If you are hiring a **private driver**, for example for the [Great Wall from Beijing](/guides/great-wall-from-beijing-layover/) or the [Terracotta Army](/guides/xian-layover-itinerary/), the driver waits with the car. Your bags stay in the vehicle, you skip storage entirely, and you save 20–30 minutes at each end.

## PVG and CAN: the airport-specific details

The counters work the same way everywhere, but the risk at each airport is different, and it is mostly about the **return leg**.

**Shanghai Pudong (PVG).** Counters sit in the arrivals and departures halls of both terminals, signed in English as "Left Luggage" or "Baggage Storage". Around **¥15–30 per bag per day**; bring your passport, and sometimes your onward ticket. The trap: the **Maglev stops around 21:40** and Metro Line 2 around **22:30**. If you are returning late, your trip back becomes a taxi or DiDi, which takes longer, so collect your bags earlier than you think you need to. PVG has two terminals connected by a walkway and the inter-terminal train, so confirm which terminal your onward flight departs from before you choose where to store. For the city side, see [things to do in Shanghai on a layover](/guides/shanghai-layover-itinerary/).

**Guangzhou Baiyun (CAN).** Counters operate in the terminal, on the arrivals level. Around **¥15–30 per bag per day**; passport required. The trap: you are coming back on **Metro Line 3**, which takes 45–55 minutes, and with a 2.5-hour departure buffer that is most of your return leg. Budget the storage detour inside that time rather than on top of it. Baiyun operates two terminals, so check which one your flight uses, because the walk between them is not trivial. For the city side, see [things to do in Guangzhou on a layover](/guides/guangzhou-layover-itinerary/).

## What to keep with you

Never store these:

- **Passport** and travel documents
- **Phone, chargers, power bank**
- **Medication**
- **Payment cards and cash**
- **Your onward ticket details** (you may need to show them at immigration)

## Practical tips

- **Photograph your bag** and note the tag number.
- **Pack valuables in a carry-on** you keep with you.
- **Do not leave bags unattended**: not in terminals, not in cafés.
- **Check the counter's closing time**; not all are 24-hour.
- **Arrive early to collect** before an international departure bank.

## Bottom line

Luggage never has to stop you leaving the airport. Use a car if you have one, a counter if you do not, and always keep documents and valuables on you. For getting into town, see [China airport-to-city transfers](/guides/china-airport-to-city-transfers/).

**Frequently asked questions**

### Can I store luggage at a Chinese airport during a layover?

Yes. Most major Chinese airports have left-luggage counters (行李寄存), usually costing around ¥15–30 per bag per day. You will need your passport and sometimes a baggage ticket.

### What is the easiest way to handle luggage on a layover?

If you are taking a private car or DiDi, keep your bags in the vehicle: the driver waits and you skip every storage step. For public transport, use airport left-luggage or your hotel.

### Do high-speed rail stations in China have luggage storage?

Many do, with staffed counters or lockers, though availability varies by station. Large stations like Shanghai Hongqiao and Beijing South generally have left-luggage services.

### Is left-luggage safe in China?

Staffed airport and station counters are generally reliable and issue a receipt, keep it. Avoid informal storage offered by individuals, and never leave bags unattended.

**Sources**

- Beijing Capital International Airport — official site: https://www.bcia.com.cn/
- Shanghai Airport — official transport information: https://www.shanghaiairport.com/
- Guangzhou Baiyun International Airport — official site: https://www.gbiac.net/

# City layover pages

## Beijing

Source: https://chinalayoverguide.com/cities/beijing/
Last updated: 2026-09-03

## Why Beijing works for a layover

Beijing is the classic first stop in China. It's not the easiest layover (the airport is far and the city is huge) but with 10+ hours you can see the imperial core and even squeeze in the Great Wall at Mutianyu if you pre-book a car or join a small group.

## The route

Take the Airport Express to Dongzhimen, then the subway to Tiananmen and the Forbidden City. Walk through to Jingshan Park for the classic view over the palace roofs. If you have a full day, head to Mutianyu early instead. It's less crowded than Badaling and the toboggan down is memorable.

## Food to try

Peking duck if you have a sit-down meal, or a quick bowl of zhajiang noodles. Street snacks near Wangfujing are fun but touristy.

## Timing notes

Forbidden City requires advance online booking with your passport and often sells out. Budget at least 90 minutes each way between PEK and the center, and more in rush hour.

---

## Chengdu

Source: https://chinalayoverguide.com/cities/chengdu/
Last updated: 2026-09-03

## Why Chengdu works for a layover

Chengdu is the best layover in western China: giant pandas in the morning, a teahouse in a park at noon, and fiery Sichuan food all day. The catch is the new Tianfu Airport is far from the city, so this route works best with 10+ hours.

## The route

Go straight to the **Chengdu Panda Base** in the morning, pandas are most active before 10am and it gets crowded later. Head back into the city for a lazy hour at **People's Park**, where you can drink tea and watch locals play mahjong. End at **Jinli Street** for snacks and souvenirs before the airport run.

## Food to try

Mapo tofu, dan dan noodles, hotpot if you're brave, and the numbing Sichuan peppercorn that makes everything buzz.

## Timing notes

Tianfu Airport is roughly an hour from the center. Pandas sleep through the afternoon, so if you can't land early, swap the panda base for Kuanzhai Alley and the park.

---

## Chongqing

Source: https://chinalayoverguide.com/cities/chongqing/
Last updated: 2026-09-16

## Why Chongqing works for a layover

Chongqing is the city that breaks the internet: monorails threading through apartment blocks, a riverside skyline stacked up hillsides, and a night view that looks like a film set. It is also the hotpot capital of China. If your route passes through western China, it is one of the most memorable short stops you can make.

## The route

Take **Metro Line 10** from Jiangbei Airport to the **Jiefangbei** area. Start at the **Liziba** viewpoint, where Line 2 runs straight through a residential building. Ride the **Yangtze River Cableway** across the river, explore the steep stairway neighborhoods, then finish at **Hongyadong**: an 11-storey stilted complex best seen illuminated at night. If you have more time, **Ciqikou** ancient town is a half-day add-on.

## Food to try

Chongqing hotpot with the nine-grid pot, chuan chuan skewers, xiaomian (spicy noodles), and suanlafen (hot-and-sour sweet potato noodles). Ask for mild if you are unsure. The default is genuinely spicy.

## Timing notes

Line 10 reaches the center in 40–50 minutes, so 8 hours is workable and 12 is comfortable. Budget extra time for the hills and traffic if you take a taxi, and be back at the airport 2.5 hours before an international departure.

## Combine with Chengdu

Chongqing and Chengdu are about 1.5 hours apart by high-speed rail, so longer transit stops can pair the two. See the [Chengdu layover guide](/cities/chengdu/) for the other half.

---

## Guangzhou

Source: https://chinalayoverguide.com/cities/guangzhou/
Last updated: 2026-09-03

## Why Guangzhou works for a layover

Guangzhou is China's food capital and one of its most relaxed big cities. It's a great layover if you're flying between Southeast Asia and Europe. The airport is huge and well connected, and the city rewards slow wandering more than checklist sightseeing.

## The route

Take Metro Line 3 to Canton Tower for the skyline, then switch to Line 6 for Shamian Island: a leafy former concession area perfect for a walk and coffee. Finish near Beijing Road for shopping and street food before heading back. If food is your priority, skip the tower and go straight to a proper dim sum lunch.

## Food to try

Dim sum (har gow, siu mai, char siu bao), roast goose, double-skin milk dessert, and anything from a busy street stall.

## Timing notes

Baiyun Airport is about 40 minutes from the center by metro. Immigration can be slow at peak hours: leave a real buffer for your onward flight.

---

## Guilin

Source: https://chinalayoverguide.com/cities/guilin/
Last updated: 2026-09-16

## Why Guilin works for a layover

Guilin is the landscape on the back of the twenty-yuan note: limestone karst peaks rising out of flat river plains. It is one of the most photographed places in China and, for travelers on a longer transit stop, one of the most rewarding.

## The route

In the city itself, start at **Elephant Trunk Hill**, then visit the **Reed Flute Cave** with its illuminated limestone formations. In the evening, the **Two Rivers and Four Lakes** area is lit up and pleasant to walk. With a full day or an overnight, add the **Li River cruise** to Yangshuo: the signature experience, and a morning departure.

## Food to try

Guilin rice noodles (*mifen*), the local staple, cheap and excellent, plus beer fish (a Yangshuo specialty) and stuffed river snails.

## Timing notes

The Li River cruise is a half-day commitment with a morning departure, so it does not fit a short layover. With 10+ hours, stick to the city sights and the evening lakes. With 24+ hours, overnight in Guilin or Yangshuo and do the river properly.

## Before you go

- [Set up a payment app](/guides/payments-in-china-for-foreigners/).
- [Install an eSIM](/guides/esim-setup-before-you-land/). This is not a city to arrive in without working maps.
- Check entry and permitted areas via [240-hour visa-free transit](/guides/240-hour-visa-free-transit/).

---

## Hangzhou

Source: https://chinalayoverguide.com/cities/hangzhou/
Last updated: 2026-09-16

## Why Hangzhou works for a layover

Hangzhou is the classic Chinese postcard: a vast lake ringed by pagodas and willow trees, temples tucked into forested hills, and tea fields on the edge of the city. It is also only about an hour from Shanghai by high-speed rail, so it works as a day trip from a Shanghai stop as well as a layover on its own.

## The route

Start at **West Lake**, walk the **Su Causeway** or the shoreline near the broken bridge. Head to **Lingyin Temple**, one of China's most important Buddhist temples, set among carvings and forest. Then visit the **Longjing (Dragon Well) tea village** for the tea terraces and a tasting. If time allows, **Hefang Street** and the illuminated **Leifeng Pagoda** round out the day.

## Food to try

Longjing shrimp (cooked with the local green tea), West Lake fish in vinegar, and Dongpo pork. Hangzhou cuisine is lighter and sweeter than Sichuan or Cantonese food.

## Timing notes

Hangzhou is compact, so a well-planned 8–10 hours is genuinely rewarding. If you are coming from Shanghai by high-speed rail, remember it departs from Hongqiao station, not the airport, and you need your passport to book and board.

## Pairing with Shanghai

A common route is to land in Shanghai, ride the high-speed train to Hangzhou for West Lake, and return. See the [Shanghai layover itinerary](/guides/shanghai-layover-itinerary/) for how to fit the transfer, and [China airport-to-city transfers](/guides/china-airport-to-city-transfers/) for the rail connections.

---

## Nanjing

Source: https://chinalayoverguide.com/cities/nanjing/
Last updated: 2026-09-16

## Why Nanjing works for a layover

Nanjing was China's capital for six dynasties and again in the twentieth century, and it carries that weight visibly, imperial tombs in forested hills, a surviving Ming city wall, and one of the country's best museums. It is also close enough to Shanghai by high-speed rail to pair with a longer stopover.

## The route

Take Metro S1 to Nanjing South and continue into the city. Start at the **Sun Yat-sen Mausoleum** and **Ming Xiaoling Mausoleum**, both set in the wooded Purple Mountain area. Then walk a stretch of the **Nanjing City Wall**, and finish in the **Confucius Temple** district for snacks and canal-side streets.

## Food to try

Salted duck (Nanjing's signature), duck blood vermicelli soup, *tangbao* soup dumplings, and sesame pastries.

## Timing notes

Lukou Airport is about 40–50 minutes out via Metro S1, and Purple Mountain deserves a couple of hours. This is a comfortable 10-hour layover rather than a quick one, with under 8 hours, focus on the City Wall and Confucius Temple area instead.

## Pairing with Shanghai

Nanjing is roughly an hour from Shanghai by high-speed rail, so a 24-hour Shanghai stopover can absorb a Nanjing day trip, see [China high-speed rail for tourists](/guides/china-high-speed-rail-for-tourists/) and the [Shanghai itinerary](/guides/shanghai-layover-itinerary/).

---

## Qingdao

Source: https://chinalayoverguide.com/cities/qingdao/
Last updated: 2026-09-16

## Why Qingdao works for a layover

Qingdao is one of China's most distinctive cities: a former German concession that left behind red-roofed villas, a cathedral, and a brewery culture that became the country's most famous beer. It sits on the Yellow Sea with a long, walkable waterfront.

## The route

Start at **Zhanqiao Pier** for the classic view of the pavilion on the water. Walk to **St. Michael's Cathedral**, then along the waterfront to the **Badaguan Scenic Area**: a district of villas and quiet tree-lined streets. Finish at the **Tsingtao Brewery Museum** for the history and a tasting, and **May Fourth Square** for the modern skyline.

## Food to try

Fresh seafood (clams, prawns, sea snails), *jiaozhi* dumplings, and of course Tsingtao beer, best drunk at a street-side beer hall in the old town.

## Timing notes

Qingdao Jiaodong Airport is about 50–60 minutes from the center by Metro Line 8, so allow for that transfer. The upside is that the classic sights are clustered along the waterfront and easily walkable. With under 6 hours, stay at the airport.

## Before you go

- [Set up a payment app](/guides/payments-in-china-for-foreigners/).
- [Install an eSIM](/guides/esim-setup-before-you-land/).
- Check entry with [can you leave the airport?](/guides/can-you-leave-the-airport-during-a-china-layover/)

---

## Shanghai

Source: https://chinalayoverguide.com/cities/shanghai/
Last updated: 2026-09-03

## Why Shanghai works for a layover

Shanghai is the easiest big-city layover in China: two airports, a Maglev train, and the country's most international downtown. If you only have one day, this route gives you the classic skyline and old-town contrast without rushing.

## The route

Start on the **Bund** for the skyline, walk 15 minutes south to **Yu Garden** for the old-town feel and a quick bite, then cut through **Nanjing Road** on your way back to Metro Line 2. If you have extra time, add a museum or the French Concession.

## Food to try

Soup dumplings (*xiaolongbao*), scallion oil noodles, and a quick *jianbing* from a street stall. Pay with Alipay/WeChat Pay, cash is increasingly rare.

## Timing notes

Pudong Airport is far from the center; budget at least 90 minutes each way. Aim for a layover of 8+ hours to make the trip worthwhile, and always leave a buffer for immigration queues.

---

## Shenzhen

Source: https://chinalayoverguide.com/cities/shenzhen/
Last updated: 2026-09-16

## Why Shenzhen works for a layover

Shenzhen is China's tech capital and one of the fastest, most modern cities in the country. It sits directly on the Hong Kong border, which makes it a natural layover for travelers routing between mainland China and Hong Kong. The airport is a genuine international hub, and the metro gets you into the thick of it quickly.

## The route

Take **Metro Line 11** from Bao'an Airport toward Futian. Start at the **Ping An Finance Centre** for the observation deck and the skyline, then head to **OCT Loft**, a converted factory district full of galleries, cafés, and design shops. Finish at **Shenzhen Bay Park** for the waterfront, or **Dongmen** for street food and shopping, before returning on Line 11.

## Food to try

Cantonese-style dim sum (Shenzhen sits in Guangdong), freshly made rice noodles, and the city's huge range of regional Chinese restaurants: the tech workforce means almost every province is represented.

## Timing notes

The airport is close by the standards of Chinese hubs: Line 11 reaches the central districts in around 30–50 minutes. Still, allow a 2.5-hour buffer before an international departure and check the last metro time. With under 6 hours, stay at the airport.

## Border note

Shenzhen has land crossings to Hong Kong (Futian, Luohu, and Shenzhen Bay). If your itinerary enters or leaves through Hong Kong, keep your onward documents handy, see [can you leave the airport during a layover?](/guides/can-you-leave-the-airport-during-a-china-layover/).

---

## Xiamen

Source: https://chinalayoverguide.com/cities/xiamen/
Last updated: 2026-09-16

## Why Xiamen works for a layover

Xiamen is one of China's most pleasant cities: a subtropical island with colonial-era architecture, a leafy university campus, and some of the best seafood on the coast. The airport is unusually close to the center, which makes it a genuinely easy layover.

## The route

Head first to **Zhongshan Road** for the pedestrian street and old-town feel, then take the **ferry to Gulangyu Island**: a car-free island of colonial villas, gardens, and viewpoints. If you are short on time, skip the island and visit **Nanputuo Temple** and **Xiamen University** instead. Finish at **Zengcuoan Village** for seafood and cafés.

## Food to try

Oyster omelette, satay noodles, fish ball soup, and the Fujian specialty *fotiaoqiang* (a complex braised soup). Xiamen is a seafood city above all.

## Timing notes

The airport is only 20–30 minutes from the center, which gives you more usable time than most Chinese hubs. But **Gulangyu ferry tickets are capacity-limited** and sell out: book online in advance and arrive early, or plan around it.

## Before you go

- [Set up a payment app](/guides/payments-in-china-for-foreigners/), island vendors are QR-only.
- [Install an eSIM](/guides/esim-setup-before-you-land/) before you fly.
- Confirm entry via [240-hour visa-free transit](/guides/240-hour-visa-free-transit/).

---

## Xi'an

Source: https://chinalayoverguide.com/cities/xian/
Last updated: 2026-09-03

## Why Xi'an works for a layover

Xi'an is the shortest route to one of the world's great sights: the Terracotta Army. If your layover is 10+ hours and you don't mind moving fast, you can see the warriors, cycle the ancient city wall, and eat your way through the Muslim Quarter in a single day.

## The route

Head straight to the **Terracotta Army**. It's an hour from the airport and gets busy by late morning. Return to the city and walk or rent a bike on the **City Wall** at the South Gate. Finish in the **Muslim Quarter** for lamb skewers and hand-pulled noodles before your flight.

## Food to try

Roujiamo (Chinese "burger"), yangrou paomo (lamb soup with crumbled bread), and the biangbiang noodles.

## Timing notes

XIY airport is about 50 minutes from the city. The Terracotta Army deserves 2–3 hours: if your layover is shorter than 10 hours, stay in the city and do the wall and Muslim Quarter instead.
